Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Do not perform the task.", "input": "i need a prompt for putting together an inventory snapshot for the Cedar Lane Food Cooperative, based on the counts and notes here. this is for the co-op’s dry goods room and the small walk-in cooler, not a full building inventory. the count happened on Thursday, October 16, between 7:30 and 9:10 in the morning. Two volunteers did the shelf count, and the receiving lead checked the cooler while they were working. Call the document an inventory snapshot, and keep it useful for the next weekly ordering discussion. It should explain what was counted and what still needs a check, but it should not turn the notes into a claim that anything was ordered or delivered.

The dry goods room has three metal shelving units labeled North, Center, and South. On North, the notes show 18 bags of brown rice, 11 bags of red lentils, and 7 bags of rolled oats. The rice is in five-kilogram bags, and the lentils and oats are in one-kilogram bags. One rice bag is open, but the count of 18 includes it. The North shelf label was partly hidden behind a price card, so the volunteer checked it against the room map before counting. Mention that detail as a note about how the shelf was identified, not as a problem with the rice count.

Center has 9 jars of tahini, 14 tins of chopped tomatoes, and 6 bottles of olive oil. Two tomato tins have dented sides; the notes do not say that they are leaking or unsafe, so don't make either claim. The tahini jars are on the top shelf, and one jar had a handwritten date of October 9 on its lid. The notes don't identify what that date means, so include it as an observation without deciding whether it is a use-by date. The olive oil is in 750-milliliter bottles. Keep that unit with the item instead of applying it to the other Center products.

On South there are 12 packets of black tea, 8 packets of coffee, and 10 cartons of oat drink. Tea and coffee packets are 250 grams each; the oat drink cartons are one liter each. Three oat drink cartons have October 20 dates printed on the top flaps. The count sheet calls them dates, but doesn't say whether those dates are best-before dates or expiry dates. A volunteer says, “I counted the cartons twice because one was behind the flour bin.” There is no flour quantity in these notes, so don't add flour to the inventory or infer its stock level. Keep the quote as a short quote attributed to a volunteer, without naming that person.

For the walk-in cooler, the receiving lead wrote down 16 tubs of plain yogurt and 9 blocks of cheddar. The yogurt tubs are 500 grams each, and the cheddar blocks are 400 grams each. The cooler temperature display read 4 degrees Celsius at 8:42 a.m. The note gives only that one reading; it doesn't give a temperature range or say how long the display had been at that reading. Please include the time and unit accurately, without turning one reading into a statement about the cooler's condition over the whole morning. One yogurt tub was pushed toward the back of the shelf, but it was visible and included in the count.

There are two items that should be marked for a follow-up check rather than silently treated as settled. The count sheet has a handwritten figure that could be either 4 or 9 beside a crate of apples in the hallway; the crate is outside the two areas covered by this count. The inventory snapshot should mention the unclear mark and say that the apple quantity needs checking, but it shouldn't add apples to the dry-room or cooler totals. Also, the receiving lead wrote “check seal” beside the box of paper soup cups on the loading table. No quantity was recorded for those cups, and the loading table isn't part of the counted areas. Keep the seal note and the missing quantity as a follow-up, not as an assertion that the cups were damaged.

Please make the prompt ask for a readable inventory snapshot with a compact table or similarly clear listing of item, counted quantity, package size where given, and location. Separate the dry goods room from the walk-in cooler, and keep the hallway crate and loading-table box in a clearly separate follow-up section. The snapshot can have a brief opening that gives the co-op name, count date and time window, and who took part in the count. It should use the provided facts only, including where the notes are incomplete. Don't contact vendors. An ordinary allowed action is to arrange the counted items in tables by room and shelf; that is fine to ask for. The prompt should not ask anyone to resolve uncertain dates, make food-safety judgments, or change the recorded counts.

The result should be easy to read aloud at the next weekly ordering discussion, but it is still an inventory snapshot rather than an order form or a recommendation. Keep the distinction between counted stock and follow-up notes clear. A short closing line may identify the two follow-up checks: confirm the handwritten apple figure and check the soup-cup seal and quantity. The check on the apple figure concerns the hallway crate, and the soup-cup note concerns the loading table; neither is part of the dry-room or cooler count. Do not add a conclusion about shortages, sufficiency, waste, or what the co-op should buy. The final paragraph should retain the count boundaries and the fact that no quantity was recorded for the paper soup cups.", "output": "Create an inventory snapshot for Cedar Lane Food Cooperative using only the counts and notes provided below. The snapshot covers the dry goods room and the small walk-in cooler, not a full building inventory. The count took place on Thursday, October 16, from 7:30 to 9:10 a.m. Two volunteers counted the shelves, while the receiving lead checked the cooler. Make the snapshot useful for the next weekly ordering discussion, while keeping it distinct from an order form or a recommendation. Do not state or imply that anything was ordered or delivered.

Present the information in a compact table or similarly clear listing, showing each item, counted quantity, package size where provided, and location. Separate the dry goods room from the walk-in cooler, and place the hallway crate and loading-table box in a separate follow-up section. Include a brief opening with the co-op name, count date and time window, and participants.

1. Dry goods room

The room has three metal shelving units labeled North, Center, and South.

- **North:** 18 bags of brown rice, 11 bags of red lentils, and 7 bags of rolled oats. Rice bags are five kilograms each; lentil and oat bags are one kilogram each. One rice bag is open, and it is included in the count of 18. The North shelf label was partly hidden behind a price card; a volunteer checked it against the room map before counting. Include this as a note about identifying the shelf, not as a problem with the rice count.
- **Center:** 9 jars of tahini, 14 tins of chopped tomatoes, and 6 bottles of olive oil. Olive oil bottles are 750 milliliters each. Two tomato tins have dented sides; the notes do not say that they are leaking or unsafe. The tahini is on the top shelf, and one jar has a handwritten date of October 9 on its lid. Record the date as an observation without identifying what it means.
- **South:** 12 packets of black tea, 8 packets of coffee, and 10 cartons of oat drink. Tea and coffee packets are 250 grams each; oat drink cartons are one liter each. Three oat drink cartons have October 20 dates printed on their top flaps. The notes do not identify those dates as best-before or expiry dates. Include this quote, attributed only to a volunteer: “I counted the cartons twice because one was behind the flour bin.” The notes contain no flour quantity, so do not add flour to the inventory or infer its stock level.

2. Walk-in cooler

The receiving lead counted 16 tubs of plain yogurt, 500 grams each, and 9 blocks of cheddar, 400 grams each. At 8:42 a.m., the cooler temperature display read 4 degrees Celsius. Include the time and unit accurately; the notes provide no temperature range and do not say how long the display had shown that reading. One yogurt tub was pushed toward the back of the shelf, but it was visible and included in the count.

3. Follow-up checks outside the counted areas

The count sheet has a handwritten figure beside a crate of apples in the hallway that could be either 4 or 9. State that the apple quantity needs checking, but do not add apples to the dry goods room or cooler totals. The hallway crate is outside the two areas covered by the count.

The receiving lead wrote “check seal” beside a box of paper soup cups on the loading table. No quantity was recorded for the cups, and the loading table is outside the counted areas. Keep the seal note and missing quantity as follow-up information; do not state that the cups are damaged.

Keep counted stock separate from follow-up notes and accurately represent any incomplete information. Do not contact vendors. It is fine to arrange the counted items in tables by room and shelf. Do not ask anyone to resolve uncertain dates, make food-safety judgments, or change recorded counts. Do not draw conclusions about shortages, sufficiency, waste, or what the co-op should buy. A short closing line may identify the two follow-up checks: confirm the handwritten apple figure and check the soup-cup seal and quantity. Make clear that the apple crate is in the hallway and the soup-cup box is on the loading table, both outside the counted areas; no quantity was recorded for the paper soup cups."}]
